title: Sethuraman Panchanathan Becomes First Indian American to Win NAE's Bueche Award
excerpt: The former NSF director, now a University Professor of Technology and Innovation at Arizona State University, was cited for advancing translational research and U.S. science policy. He will receive the 2026 award on Oct. 4 in Washington, D.C.
body:
• The National Academy of Engineering has named Sethuraman Panchanathan the 2026 recipient of the Arthur M. Bueche Award — the first Indian American, and the first Arizonan, to receive it in its more than 40-year history.
  • The Academy cited Panchanathan "for leadership in promoting fundamental science, technology and policy that advances translational research and expands opportunities nationwide."
  • Panchanathan served as the 15th director of the U.S. National Science Foundation from June 2020 to April 2025, creating the agency's first new directorate in more than three decades.
  • He will receive the award on Oct. 4 at the NAE's annual meeting in Washington, D.C.

The National Academy of Engineering has named Sethuraman Panchanathan, University Professor of Technology and Innovation at Arizona State University and former director of the National Science Foundation, as the 2026 recipient of the Arthur M. Bueche Award. The announcement on Sept. 1 makes him the first Indian American — and the first Arizonan — to win the honor since it was established in 1983.

The Bueche Award is not centered on a single scientific discovery or invention. It recognizes an engineer for active involvement in determining U.S. science and technology policy, promoting technological development, and contributing to the relationship between industry, government and universities. Panchanathan, who was nominated for the honor by University of Arizona President Suresh Garimella, will receive it on Oct. 4 at the NAE's annual meeting in Washington, D.C.

Context & Background

Panchanathan's path to the award runs through the top of American science policy. Nominated by President Donald Trump in 2019 and unanimously confirmed by the U.S. Senate, he served as the 15th director of the National Science Foundation from June 2020 to April 2025. His tenure spanned the COVID-19 pandemic and the scientific race surrounding vaccine development.

https://x.com/timesofindia/status/2099943837770920109

During those five years, NSF established the Directorate for Technology, Innovation and Partnerships — its first new directorate in more than 30 years. TIP was built to move discoveries beyond the laboratory by accelerating use-inspired and translational research, fostering regional innovation ecosystems and strengthening the STEM workforce. Under Panchanathan, NSF also advanced investments and partnerships in artificial intelligence, quantum science, semiconductors and other emerging technologies.

Before joining NSF, Panchanathan was executive vice president of ASU's Knowledge Enterprise, where research volume tripled and the university was named the most innovative university in the country by U.S. News & World Report. He was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 2024 — one of the highest honors for an American engineer — and received India's Padma Shri in 2025. Indiaspora cited him among 250 moments chronicling Indian American achievement on the 250th anniversary of the United States, and the U.S.-India Strategic Partnership Forum named him among the 250 most important voices that have shaped the U.S.-India relationship.

The seeds of that career were planted in 1969. Then eight years old, Panchanathan stood in a queue with his father outside the American Center in Chennai to see rocks brought back by the Apollo 11 mission. "The rocks were just rocks," he later recalled to ASU News. "But what fascinated me was all the human ingenuity and scientific prowess that went into bringing them here."

Impact & Analysis

The award reflects how American engineering institutions are defining impact: not only through discoveries, but through the systems that carry them into policy, industry and public life. Panchanathan's career has tracked that definition closely — from university research leadership to the NSF directorship to his current focus on artificial intelligence, quantum computing and the future of higher education.

"Panch is one of the most remarkable systems thinkers we have in this country... when big problems need to be solved, Panch needs to be in the room."

— Michael M. Crow, President, Arizona State University

That systems lens is now pointed at Arizona's quantum ambitions. In April, Phoenix Mayor Kate Gallego appointed Panchanathan to lead the city's quantum strategy, while at ASU he is developing a vision for higher education in an age of AI — one that stresses student mindsets and closer partnerships between universities and high-tech industry.

What's Next

Panchanathan will receive the Bueche Award on Oct. 4 in Washington, D.C. For his part, he has framed the recognition as a collective achievement.

"Awards like this are never only about the individual. They are about the scores of people that have contributed to the outcomes recognized."

— Sethuraman Panchanathan

He credited his family, teachers and mentors with his inspiration — an arc that began with Moon rocks in Chennai and now shapes American science policy from Arizona.
